summary: Describes procedures for distributing upstream-assigned labels in LDP. It also shows how they can avoid having a branching router replicate traffic on a LAN for LDP point-to-multipoint paths.

eli5.summary: Normally the receiver picks the label. Here the sender picks it instead, which saves making many copies of the same message on a shared network.

questions: what is upstream label assignment in ldp
what is the ldp upstream label assignment capability
how does ldp avoid replication on a lan
subtitle: How LDP routers hand out labels chosen by the sender, so a branch router can send one copy on a shared LAN.

tldr.problem: On a LAN, an LDP point-to-multipoint LSP relies on ingress replication, so a branch router sends a separate copy of each packet to every downstream router.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6389 adds an LDP capability and two TLVs so a router can advertise and distribute upstream-assigned labels, and uses them so the branch router sends a single copy on the LAN.
tldr.outcome: Branch routers can avoid per-neighbor replication on a LAN when downstream routers support upstream label assignment, while other routers keep using ingress replication. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6389 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2011, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 5331 and RFC 6388.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document describes procedures for distributing upstream-assigned labels (RFC 5331) for the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP, RFC 5036). It follows the architecture in RFC 5331.

It defines LDP extensions that let a Label Switching Router (LSR) tell its neighbors whether it supports upstream label assignment, and extensions to distribute the labels themselves. It also describes how to use upstream label assignment to avoid branch LSR traffic replication on a LAN for LDP point-to-multipoint (P2MP) Label Switched Paths (LSPs) from RFC 6388.
sections.eli5: In most label systems the receiver tells the sender which label to use. This document lets the sender choose the label, and shows why that helps on a shared network.

sections.title: The Upstream Label Assignment Capability
sections.content:
RFC 5331 says upstream-assigned label bindings MUST NOT be used unless it is known that the downstream LSR supports them. So an LSR needs a way to advertise support. RFC 6389 defines a new Capability Parameter, the LDP Upstream Label Assignment Capability, following the format and procedures of RFC 5561. Its type is 0x0507, its length is 1, and the value is one set bit followed by seven reserved bits.

Including it in LDP Initialization messages means the LSR can both distribute and receive upstream-assigned label bindings. The reserved bits MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt. The parameter MUST be carried only in Initialization messages and MUST be ignored if it arrives in LDP Capability messages.
sections.eli5: Before sending a special kind of label, a router first checks that its neighbor said "yes, I understand those" when they first said hello.

sections.title: The New TLVs
sections.content:
Two optional LDP TLVs are introduced. The Upstream-Assigned Label Request TLV (0x0205) MUST be included in a Label Request message to ask for an upstream-assigned label. The Upstream-Assigned Label TLV (0x0204) signals the label and is carried in messages that advertise, release and withdraw upstream-assigned label mappings.

The Label field is a 20-bit label value as specified in RFC 3032, represented as a 20-bit number in a 4-octet field as in RFC 5036.
sections.eli5: There are two new kinds of note. One says "please let me pick a label", and the other carries the label that was picked.

sections.title: Distribution Procedures
sections.content:
Label Mapping, Label Request, Label Abort, Label Withdraw and Label Release follow RFC 5036 except for the changes in this section. An LSR MUST NOT send either new TLV to a neighbor that has not advertised the capability in its Initialization messages. Distribution of upstream-assigned labels is similar to either ordered or independent LSP control of downstream-assigned labels.

A Label Mapping with an upstream-assigned label MUST include the Upstream-Assigned Label TLV. A receiver that does not recognize the TLV MUST send a Notification with status "Unknown TLV". One that recognizes it but cannot process the label MUST send "No Label Resources". If the mapping answers a request, that request MUST have contained the Upstream-Assigned Label Request TLV.

An LSR that sends an upstream-assigned label request for a FEC MUST NOT send a downstream label mapping for that FEC to the same neighbor unless it withdraws the upstream binding. The reverse also holds: after a downstream-assigned request, no upstream mapping unless that request is aborted. The Upstream-Assigned Label TLV may optionally appear in Label Withdraw and Label Release messages.
sections.eli5: The rule is to ask for only one kind of label per topic at a time. A router must not hand out the sender-picked kind and the receiver-picked kind for the same thing together.

sections.title: Tunnel Identifier Exchange
sections.content:
An upstream LSR (Ru) may send a packet whose top label is upstream assigned over a tunnel to its downstream neighbor (Rd). Rd knows the label is upstream assigned from the tunnel the packet arrives on, so Ru must tell Rd which tunnel it will use. In LDP this is done with the Interface ID TLV of RFC 3472. If Ru uses an IP or MPLS tunnel, it MUST include that TLV in Label Mapping messages along with the Upstream-Assigned Label TLV. The IPv4 form has type 0x082d and the IPv6 form 0x082e. The next/previous hop address and Logical Interface ID fields SHOULD be set to 0 and ignored by the receiver.

The Interface ID TLV carries sub-TLVs, and four new ones identify the tunnel: the RSVP-TE P2MP LSP TLV (type 28), the LDP P2MP LSP TLV (type 29), the IP Multicast Tunnel TLV (type 30) and the MPLS Context Label TLV (type 31). The Context Label TLV is limited to LDP P2MP LSPs on a LAN and MUST NOT be used for any other purpose.
sections.eli5: The sender has to say which road the special packets will travel on, so the receiver knows how to read their labels.

sections.title: LDP P2MP LSPs on a LAN
sections.content:
With RFC 6388 on a LAN, a branch LSR (Ru) sends a separate copy of each packet to every adjacent downstream LSR. This is called ingress replication. It is desirable for Ru to send one copy, which requires each downstream LSR to associate the label Ru uses on the LAN with the P2MP LSP.

If Rd finds that the upstream interface to the root is a LAN interface and both Rd and Ru support upstream-assigned labels, Rd sends a Label Request containing an Upstream-Assigned Label Request TLV instead of a normal Label Mapping. Ru replies with a Label Mapping carrying an upstream-assigned label and an Interface ID TLV with an MPLS Context Label sub-TLV, assigned by Ru on the LAN interface. If several downstream LSRs request the same P2MP FEC, Ru MUST send the same label to each.

Ru then sends packets with the context label as the top label and the upstream-assigned LSP label below it. Downstream LSRs use the top label, looked up in the context of the LAN interface, to find the label space for the inner label.

When there are several equal-cost next hops on the LAN, downstream LSRs MAY pick one upstream LSR by numbering the candidates from lower to higher IP address and computing H = (Sum Opaque value) modulo N, where N is the number of candidates. LSRs that do not support upstream label assignment keep using ingress replication and downstream label assignment.
sections.eli5: Instead of mailing the same letter to each neighbor on a street, the sender pins one copy on a shared board with a label everyone agrees to read.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of RFC 5036, RFC 5331 and RFC 5332 apply. The RFC also points to RFC 5920 for a more detailed discussion of security threats, defensive techniques and detection and reporting mechanisms for MPLS and GMPLS networks.
sections.eli5: It adds no new safety rules of its own. The safety rules of the systems it builds on still apply.
